deck.headline: Lean experts certify Anthropic mathematician's Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as correct
deck.sub: A day after Levent Alpöge released a 17-million-line Lean proof, the Lean and Mathlib communities say every check passed. Mathematicians now have to understand the ideas.
deck.summary: The Lean and Mathlib communities certify that Levent Alpöge's 17-million-line Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, made with Anthropic's Claude, is correct. Independent checkers, two formally proven unable to accept a false proof, accepted it. The certificate covers the Riemann Hypothesis, not his separate GRH claim; experts still have to explain the ideas.
deck.whyItMatters: A 167-year-old problem has a machine-checked proof found with an AI model, which is a strong signal that AI plus formal verification can produce results nobody has to take on trust. It does not break today's encryption; the practical lesson for banks is about verification, not cryptography.
deck.update: The Lean and Mathlib communities, backed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, certify (21 Nov) that Levent Alpöge's 17-million-line Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, after independent proof checkers and two statement-matching tools all passed.
deck.checked: Opened the Lean community's joint statement and Andrew Sutherland's MIT verification page; both describe the same checks. Not checked by us: the proof itself.
deck.detailHtml:
Yesterday's claim has passed the formal test. In a joint statement endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, the Lean and Mathlib communities say they have full confidence that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct and "hereby certify" both the statement and the proof. The proof is a Lean library of about 17 million lines that depends only on Mathlib. Their checks: the statement of RH is the one already in Mathlib, vetted by Lean and number-theory experts; dozens of people compiled the library and got the same proof export; two independent tools confirmed the theorem proved is exactly Mathlib's RH; and the export was accepted by Lean's own kernel and several independent checkers in different languages, including con-leche and con-ron, which come with formal proofs that they cannot accept a false proof. The checks ran on an inert export, out of reach of any malicious code in the sources. MIT's Andrew Sutherland, who ran his checks with Claude Code, reports all 175,187 modules compile, the five headline theorems use only Lean's three standard axioms, and the nanoda and con-leche kernels accept the full export. The community statement covers RH; it does not mention the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis that Alpöge also claimed, and the human explanation of the new ideas is still to come.

On Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said that working with an internal Claude model for about six weeks he had proved the Riemann Hypothesis, and released the proof as Lean code. Normally a claimed proof of a famous conjecture takes referees months or years. Here the proof was written in a language a computer can check, so the question became narrower: does it compile, does it prove the right statement, and can the checker be trusted?

Within a day the Lean and Mathlib communities answered all three. The statement matches the one already in Mathlib; independent people rebuilt the 17-million-line library and got the same export; two tools confirmed the statement; and several independently written checkers, two of them formally proven unable to accept a false proof, accepted it. What remains is human work: understanding why the proof works and what new mathematics it contains.

deck.headline: Planted secrets show AI providers leaking prompts, and one host's model was secretly swapped
deck.summary: Dragos seeded about two million prompts with fake credentials and found attackers stealing data from three AI hosting providers, resellers keeping customer prompts and zero-retention settings ignored. Separately, Prime Intellect says a hacker swapped its DeepSeek model for a refusal-free copy for 53 hours. The affected providers in Dragos's study are not named.
deck.whyItMatters: Banks sending customer or deal data to AI models through routers, marketplaces or small hosts should assume a privacy flag is not a control. Map every route a prompt takes, prefer direct contracts with named providers, and seed your own canaries.
deck.checked: Opened Dragos's report and Prime Intellect's security advisory (both official), plus CryptoSlate's write-up of the swap and Ars Technica's security page; The Defiant (Together AI) was blocked.
deck.storyline: Storyline: who sees your AI prompts · day 1
deck.detailHtml: Dragos's research team, led by HD Moore, sent about two million prompts containing unique URLs and fake credentials to widely used AI services between July and November, then watched where they surfaced. It found attackers actively stealing data from three hosting providers (the earliest from mid-July); bait AWS keys were used for tens of thousands of API calls, and one attacker who had hit two providers at once added the ARTEX AI hacking tool on 1 November. Resellers on an inference marketplace could read and keep customer prompts using ordinary logging, and several providers appeared to ignore privacy settings, including zero data retention: prompts sent to US providers reached Chinese organisations, and one seeded link turned up in an internal company chat in China. Dragos does not name the providers in the sections we read. Separately, Prime Intellect discloses that an unauthorised party replaced its DeepSeek V4.1 Flash deployment with a copy modified to stop refusing, from 8 Nov 01:24 to 10 Nov 06:35 UTC; HarmBench refusals fell from 198 of 240 to zero while capability scores were unchanged. It says it found no sign prompts were recorded. The Defiant reports Together AI disclosed a prompt leak after the study; we could not open that report.

deck.headline: Microsoft says attackers read tenant data through a flaw in Entra Connect Health
deck.summary: Microsoft says attackers exploited a flaw in its Entra Connect Health service, live from 23 July until a fix on 19 November, to read tenant metadata such as admin email addresses, tenant IDs and licence details. It says no passwords, tokens or valid keys were exposed. Only one outlet has reported the customer notice so far.
deck.whyItMatters: Banks running hybrid identity should check the Microsoft 365 admin centre for the notice and expect targeted phishing at the named admin addresses; the data is a map of who runs your identity stack.
deck.checked: Opened BleepingComputer's report, which quotes Microsoft's customer notification; no public Microsoft advisory found on re-search.
deck.detailHtml: Microsoft is telling customers that attackers exploited a vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API, the cloud service that monitors on-premises identity servers, according to a notification shared by admins and reported by BleepingComputer. The flaw was introduced on 23 July, found on 9 November and fixed server-side on 19 November. Microsoft says attackers got read-only access to tenant metadata: email addresses of administrators and technical contacts, tenant IDs and names, domains, country and region, Entra licence tier and directory-sync status, plus an expired certificate once used to register Connect Health agents. It says no passwords, hashes, tokens, valid keys, Active Directory topology or Azure subscription data were exposed and no configuration changes were found. It has not said how many tenants were hit; several managed service providers received notices for multiple customers. No customer action is required, the notice says.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGBleepingComputer: Microsoft Entra Connect Health flaw exploited to steal tenant data

deck.headline: Amazon nears a $7.5bn deal for Decart, maker of real-time video and world models
deck.summary: Amazon is close to buying Decart, the Israeli startup behind the Lucy real-time video model and Oasis world models, for about $7.5bn, the FT reports. Decart was valued near $4bn in May. Neither company has confirmed the deal, which would put world-model technology inside Amazon's cloud.
deck.whyItMatters: World models are becoming a cloud product; if AWS buys one, expect simulation and synthetic-video tools inside its AI stack, and more pressure on rivals' prices for the few teams that build them.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI models of 3D worlds · day 5
deck.detailHtml: Amazon is nearing a deal to buy Decart, an Israeli AI startup, for about $7.5bn, the Financial Times reported on Saturday (via The Information). The Wall Street Journal first reported talks last month at around $7bn. The product is the point: Decart's Lucy model edits video in real time, and its Oasis models generate simulated worlds used to train and test robots and self-driving systems. PitchBook data cited by the WSJ put Decart near $4bn in May, after a $300m round led by Radical Ventures that brought in Nvidia. Earlier reports said other buyers had looked and walked away. Neither company has confirmed a deal.

deck.headline: Spain will extend its bank levy through 2027 to pay for housing, Sánchez says
deck.summary: Spain's prime minister Pedro Sánchez says his cabinet will approve on Tuesday an extension of the bank levy through 2027, raising about €1.4bn for social housing, tenant incentives and renovation. The announcement comes eight days before the 29 November snap election, and a new government could change it.
deck.whyItMatters: Spain's big lenders face another year of the levy in their 2027 plans, and politicians elsewhere are watching a tax on bank income sold as housing money; banks with European franchises should model it.
deck.detailHtml: Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Saturday that his cabinet will approve on Tuesday an extension of the current banking levy to 2027 and that its revenue, about €1.4bn, will all go to housing: social housing, incentives for tenants and home renovation, Reuters reports. "We will extend the bank tax, and the revenue will go towards" housing, he said. Sánchez called a snap election for 29 November to ride the momentum of mass housing protests. A government formed after the vote could change course, and the detailed terms have not been published.

deck.headline: UN talks on a binding treaty for autonomous weapons collapse in Geneva
deck.summary: UN talks in Geneva failed to agree a mandate for a binding treaty on autonomous weapons after an all-night session. More than 100 states wanted one, but Russia blocked consensus and the US and other military powers preferred nonbinding rules. Countries will instead work on an instrument that may carry no legal obligations.
deck.whyItMatters: There will be no global legal limit on AI that selects and attacks targets for years; defence-tech lending and investment will keep running on national rules and company policies.
deck.storyline: Storyline: rules for military AI · day 1
deck.detailHtml: After a week of talks and an all-night session, the UN's Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva failed just before 5am on Saturday to agree a mandate to negotiate a legally binding treaty on autonomous weapons, the Guardian reports. More than 100 states wanted a new law, but the forum works by consensus. Russia led the objections with stalling tactics, and the US and other powers investing in AI warfare, including South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany, preferred a nonbinding approach. The conference instead asked countries "to elaborate by consensus" an instrument that may carry no legal obligations. The US said human control over such weapons came up between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at Apec this week.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGThe Guardian: international UN talks on controlling autonomous weapons collapse · The Verge: the UN fails to agree on rules regulating 'killer robots'

deck.headline: FBI's national crime database and a USDA payments system are reported hacked
deck.summary: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, the database police use to check warrants and stolen property, CNN reports; it is the second reported FBI breach in two months. A separate hack of a US agriculture payments database is disrupting farm payments. How attackers got in is unknown.
deck.whyItMatters: Banks that rely on government data feeds or pay out farm and subsidy money should watch for delays and fraud attempts that exploit the confusion.
deck.storyline: Storyline: data breaches at public bodies · day 2
deck.detailHtml: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center (NCIC), the database police across the US use during traffic stops and investigations to check warrants, missing persons, stolen vehicles and protection orders, CNN reported, citing two people briefed. It is the second reported FBI breach in two months, after ShinyHunters claimed an attack through an Oracle PeopleSoft flaw. It is not known when or how attackers got in, or whether data was taken; President Trump confirmed the hack in a Fox News interview. Separately, NBC and Reuters report an intrusion into a US Department of Agriculture payments database, which former officials warn could open a path to more sensitive data; local reports say farm payments are disrupted as a 11 December sign-up deadline nears.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGBleepingComputer: FBI reportedly hacked again, this time targeting nationwide police database · The Verge: the FBI and USDA were reportedly hacked

deck.headline: Rackspace Spot breach let attackers read customers' Kubernetes secrets for most of a day
deck.summary: Rackspace says attackers used leaked credentials to get into its Rackspace Spot Kubernetes cloud for most of 17 November, where they could create pods and read customers' Kubernetes Secrets, which hold passwords and API keys. Customers are told to rotate every stored credential. Only one outlet has the notice so far.
deck.whyItMatters: A breach at a cloud host becomes a breach of every system whose keys sat in its clusters; vendor-risk teams should ask Kubernetes providers how quickly they can force secret rotation.
deck.storyline: Storyline: attacks through software and vendors · day 8
deck.detailHtml: Rackspace says an unauthorised party used leaked credentials to get into parts of Rackspace Spot, its managed Kubernetes cloud, from about 00:20 to 22:00 UTC on 17 November, according to a customer notice obtained by BleepingComputer. Acting as legitimate users in some customer organisations, the attackers could create pods, read Kubernetes Secrets (where apps keep database passwords, API keys and tokens) and list nodes and volumes, and could have read any Spot API or refresh token the user held. Rackspace learned of it from a customer on 18 November, revoked tokens, removed the pods and rotated keys. It tells customers to reissue tokens, download fresh configs, rotate every credential stored in cluster Secrets and review logs for databases, registries, Git and cloud storage back to 17 November.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGBleepingComputer: Rackspace Spot breach let hackers access customer Kubernetes secrets

deck.headline: Researchers show one malicious webpage could hijack Meta's Muse agent and its stored logins
deck.summary: Security firm NebuSec showed that one malicious webpage could make Meta's Muse agent send a user's chats and memories to an outside server without asking, and that chained bugs gave full control of the user's cloud machine and its stored logins. It was a lab test, and NebuSec says Meta has fixed every flaw.
deck.whyItMatters: Agents that hold customers' bank logins are now a target in their own right; banks should treat agent platforms as third parties with access to accounts and press for proof of isolation.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI agents for consumers · day 11
deck.detailHtml: Researchers at NebuSec showed that a malicious webpage opened by Meta's Muse, the personal agent that works through users' connected accounts and can make purchases, could copy a user's conversation history and stored memories to an outside server and alter them with no approval prompt, The Hacker News reports. They then chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser to a Linux kernel bug to take full control of the user's cloud machine, reaching the credential store, saved files and Sentinel, the monitoring layer meant to be the single gate for what the agent sends out. It was a lab demonstration inside the researchers' own accounts, not an attack on users, and NebuSec says Meta has fixed every weakness it describes. Earlier this week Meta staff found Muse surfacing strangers' bank balances in internal tests.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGThe Hacker News: a single malicious webpage let researchers hijack Meta Muse

stat.label: all flaws, NebuSec says; lab-only test

deck.headline: GnuPG patches a critical GPGME bug that a booby-trapped key can trigger
deck.summary: GnuPG released GPGME 2.3.1 to fix CVE-2026-129975, a critical bug in every earlier version: a booby-trapped OpenPGP key can make apps that use the library leak data, and code execution can't be ruled out. Mail clients, Samba and Gpg4win are affected. No attacks are reported yet.
deck.whyItMatters: Banks use GnuPG for file transfers with counterparties and regulators; patch GPGME and Gpg4win on transfer servers and desktops now.
deck.storyline: Storyline: attacks through software and vendors · day 8
deck.detailHtml: The GnuPG project released GPGME 2.3.1 on Friday to fix CVE-2026-129975, which it calls a critical bug in all earlier versions. An OpenPGP key with a crafted, very long user ID triggers a double free in two routines that read output from gpg; the project says this can be used to exfiltrate data from applications, for example by sending signed data, and that remote code execution can't be ruled out. GPGME is the library most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba and GnuPG's own Gpg4win and GnuPG Desktop use to talk to GnuPG; new versions of those were released too. Johan Carlsson found it and GitLab reported it on 12 November; disclosure moved up from 25 November because GitLab had to ship early for the Ruby2Shell bug. No attacks are reported. Separately, pwn.ai published Upload2Shell (CVE-2026-125396), a Ghostscript sandbox escape reachable through document and image uploads, fixed upstream in Ghostscript 10.08.0 in September.

deck.headline: Kalshi faces a Monday hearing on a New York order it says would shut it down
deck.summary: A federal judge rejected the CFTC's second emergency bid to halt New York's case against Kalshi, so a state court will hear on Monday an order Kalshi says would shut its exchange nationwide. New York's attorney general says that is not her aim. The case alleges unlicensed gambling.
deck.whyItMatters: Brokers and banks partnering with prediction markets face a real chance that the biggest US venue is restricted by a state court before federal rules settle.
deck.storyline: Storyline: prediction markets and their rules · day 8
deck.detailHtml: A federal judge in Manhattan on Friday denied the CFTC's second emergency request to stop New York Attorney General Letitia James from pursuing her case against Kalshi, sending the fight to a New York state court on Monday, Crypto Briefing reports. That court will weigh an order that Kalshi says would shut down its exchange nationwide, since the company is headquartered in New York; James has said that is not her goal, per The Block. Her July lawsuit alleges Kalshi runs unlicensed gambling under state law. It adds to appeals-court losses for Kalshi in other states this month.

deck.headline: Mexico captures FBI-wanted cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro'; at least 11 killed
deck.summary: Mexican forces, helped by US intelligence, captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, 'El Chapo Isidro', one of the FBI's ten most wanted, in Sinaloa after an overnight gun battle. At least 11 people died in the violence that followed. He was flown to Mexico City.
deck.whyItMatters: A high-profile US-Mexico security win as the US presses Mexico on cartels; expect retaliation risk in Sinaloa and possible extradition moves.
deck.detailHtml: Mexican forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro" and one of the FBI's ten most wanted fugitives, in Guasave, Sinaloa, and flew him to Mexico City on Saturday after a heavy overnight firefight that left trucks and businesses burning, AP reports. The operation was run by Mexico's defence ministry with US intelligence agencies. At least 11 people died in the violence, including seven alleged cartel gunmen. Meza Flores rose through the Beltrán-Leyva cartel before leading his own group.

deck.headline: COP31 climate talks deadlock over fossil fuels and run past their deadline
deck.summary: COP31 in Turkey ran more than a day past its deadline and was suspended in deadlock. The EU and Pacific islands reject a draft with no mention of cutting fossil-fuel demand, and African countries want more adaptation money. Without consensus the summit could end with no deal, only the second time since 1995.
deck.whyItMatters: A weak or failed COP removes a push behind transition-finance targets; banks with net-zero lending commitments face less policy cover and more scrutiny.
deck.detailHtml: Talks at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, were in deadlock and suspended for the night on Saturday after running more than a day over time, the BBC reports. The EU and Pacific island nations are pushing back against a draft that makes no reference to reducing demand for fossil fuels; EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said that without "what is needed" there is "no deal". The Africa Group wants more money for adaptation, which the EU has said it will not support. Negotiators due to fly home on Sunday moved flights to Monday. Without consensus the summit could end with no deal and reconvene next year, which has happened only once since 1995. An earlier draft, Reuters reported, had dropped language on phasing out fossil fuels.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGBBC: fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock · Arab News (Reuters): COP31 draft climate deal removes mention of fossil fuels

deck.headline: Trump says Huang should apologise and return to Nvidia; the board says no
deck.summary: President Trump says Jensen Huang should apologise and be allowed back as Nvidia's chief executive, but the board says it has no plans to rehire him. Bloomberg reports California's probe now covers possible criminal violations, which we could not open. Nvidia ended the week near $126 after a 14% Friday fall.
deck.whyItMatters: Political pressure now pulls against the board's governance clean-up; lenders and index investors should expect more volatility until the 10-Q and the board's answers to Treasury arrive.
deck.update: Trump says (20 Nov) Jensen Huang should apologise and be allowed to return as CEO; Nvidia's board says it has no plans to bring him back; Bloomberg reports California's probe now covers potential criminal violations (headline only).
deck.detailHtml: President Donald Trump said on Friday that Jensen Huang should apologise and be allowed to return as Nvidia's chief executive, DigiTimes reports. Nvidia's board has said plainly it has no plans to bring him back, even as some tech executives push for it, Crypto Briefing notes. Bloomberg reports that California's investigation into whether Nvidia misled investors about China risks now extends to potential criminal violations; we saw only the headline. Nvidia closed the week near $126 after Friday's 14% fall on reports that the SEC is examining its accounting.

alsoToday.headline: Hong Kong bill would license crypto custodians, dealers and advisers
alsoToday.summary: Hong Kong's government published the Virtual Asset Services Legislation (Amendment) Bill 2026 on Friday, which would require firms doing four activities, dealing, advising, managing and custody of crypto assets, to be licensed by or registered with the SFC, extending oversight beyond trading platforms, Cointelegraph reports.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Banks offering crypto custody or advice in Hong Kong will need to map their activities onto the new licence categories.

alsoToday.detailHtml: Hong Kong's government published the Virtual Asset Services Legislation (Amendment) Bill 2026 on Friday, which would require firms doing four activities, dealing, advising, managing and custody of crypto assets, to be licensed by or registered with the SFC, extending oversight beyond trading platforms, Cointelegraph reports. alsoToday.headline: Alcaraz fights back to meet world number one Zverev in the ATP Finals final
alsoToday.summary: Carlos Alcaraz came back to beat Ben Shelton 3-6 6-3 7-6 (7-1), playing with strapping on an injured hamstring, and will face world number one Alexander Zverev in Sunday's ATP Finals final in Turin after Zverev beat Daniil Medvedev 7-6 (7-0) 6-4, the BBC reports.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: The season ends with the top two rivals meeting, and Alcaraz's fitness is the open question.
alsoToday.detailHtml: Carlos Alcaraz came back to beat Ben Shelton 3-6 6-3 7-6 (7-1), playing with strapping on an injured hamstring, and will face world number one Alexander Zverev in Sunday's ATP Finals final in Turin after Zverev beat Daniil Medvedev 7-6 (7-0) 6-4, the BBC reports. Alcaraz, on a 13-match winning streak, is chasing his first title at the season-ending event.

alsoToday.headline: Pant's century puts India 261 ahead in the first Test in Wellington
alsoToday.summary: Rishabh Pant made 128, his ninth Test century, from 135 balls for his hundred, before falling one ball before lunch on day four in Wellington, AP reports. India were 629-6 at the break, 261 ahead of New Zealand's first-innings 368, with Dhruv Jurel 32 not out.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: India are in control of the first Test going into the last day and a half.
